questions.question: What does range(5) produce?
questions.answer:
It produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, because the stop value 5 is exclusive (not included).

code:
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

real example:
Repeating an action exactly five times, like five retry attempts.

questions.question:
What does this print?
first = [1, 2, 3]
for x in first:
    first.append(x)  # careful!
print(first)
questions.answer:
It never finishes. Appending while iterating over the same list keeps the list growing, so the loop runs forever.

code:
first = [1, 2, 3]
for x in first.copy():
    first.append(x)
print(first)

real example:
Always loop over a copy when you plan to grow a list during iteration.

break stops the loop the moment i reaches 1, so only 0 prints.

continue skips the current iteration for i == 2, so the loop prints 0, 1, 3, 4.

code:

The loop runs normally to completion, so the else block prints done after 0, 1, 2.

code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
else:
    print("done")

real example:
Confirming a file was fully processed when no break occurred.

break on finding 3 skips the else, so only found 3 prints.

code:

for n in nums:

else:

real example:

questions.question:
What does this print?
word = "racecar"
is_pal = True
for i in range(len(word) // 2):
    if word[i] != word[-(i + 1)]:
        is_pal = False
        break
print(is_pal)
questions.answer:
The loop compares outer letters with inner letters, and racecar matches at every step, so True prints.

code:
word = "racecar"
print(word == word[::-1])

real example:
Checking whether a serial number reads the same backwards.
